title: A new commandment (John 13:34–35)
hook: love one another as I have loved you; by this all will know

segments.voice: Yesterday, the towel, and Peter learning to be served. Your line was not only my feet. Did you let someone help you? Day five hundred seventeen.

How do you spot a team's fans in an airport? The jersey. A nurse? The scrubs, the clip-on badge. A soldier, a chef, a judge: there's usually something you can see. Uniforms answer the question, who are you with? Judas has just gone out into the night, John says. The door closes behind him. And Jesus, with the eleven who are left, tells them how people will be able to pick them out of a crowd. It isn't a uniform.
screen: `THE JERSEY, THE SCRUBS.` → `JUDAS GOES OUT INTO THE NIGHT.` → `NOT A UNIFORM.`

segments.voice: Here are the words, in the Douay-Rheims: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." The first thing to ask is, what's new about it? Love of neighbor isn't new. It's already in Leviticus: thou shalt love thy friend as thyself, as the Douay renders it, and Jesus quotes it himself in the other Gospels. The new part is the measure. Not as you love yourself, but as I have loved you. And how has he loved them? An hour ago he was on his knees with a towel, washing their feet. Within a day he'll lay down his life. That's the yardstick now. The second thing is the sign. All men will know. Not by a creed recited, or a building, or a badge, but by something people can watch from outside: how these people treat each other. Around the year 200, the North African writer Tertullian reported how outsiders talked about Christians in his city: look how they love one another, they said, and how ready they are to die for each other. That's the commandment working as a sign. The Latin for commandment is mandatum, and that word gave Holy Thursday its old English name, Maundy Thursday. On that night, as the priest washes feet, the Church traditionally sings an antiphon that begins, in Latin, mandatum novum: a new commandment.
screen: `NOT NEW: LEVITICUS ALREADY SAID IT.` · `NEW: AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `A SIGN OUTSIDERS CAN SEE.` · `MANDATUM: MAUNDY THURSDAY.` · then, large: `A NEW COMMANDMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one visible act of love. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'll actually see today, at home, at work, at school, in a group chat. Pick one. Now pick one thing you could do for them that someone else might notice: standing up for them in a meeting, clearing their plate, a public thank you, sitting with the person nobody sits with. Picture yourself doing it. If you pray, you can hold the line, as I have loved you. If you don't, just hold that one person. The bell holds the time.
Mandatum. The Latin for commandment, the root of Maundy Thursday: love one another as Jesus loved them, with a towel and a cross. Today's word.
Your line: by this they will know. Today, do your one visible act of love, and let it be seen. Day five hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: At the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper, the Church sings antiphons during the washing of feet, traditionally including one drawn from John 13:34, "Mandatum novum," a new commandment.

original.note: Greek: a new commandment (John 13:34). Latin: mandatum novum.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to each other.
what it means: love measured by how Jesus loved, kneeling and dying, as the one sign that marks his disciples.
what a scholar hears: kainē suggests new in kind; the Latin mandatum gave Maundy Thursday its name; Tertullian's Apology 39 records outsiders saying, see how they love one another.
